steps.title: Count failed, unknown-account and successful logins
steps.do: Drop the cursor to the fresh prompt line at the bottom of the window, then type grep -c "Failed password" auth-jump01.log while speaking, with no pause, then press Return. Rest the cursor on the 53 in the output. Drift the cursor down beside the next prompt line, then type grep -c "invalid user" auth-jump01.log while speaking, with no pause, then press Return. Slide the cursor down onto the 14 in the output. Move the cursor between the 53 and the 14: these are the bar the pivot has to hit, and if the pivot is not 53, a row went astray. Slide the cursor down the left side of the text to the new prompt, then type grep 'Accepted' auth-jump01.log (Accepted in single quotes) while speaking, with no pause, then press Return. Sweep the cursor down the six Accepted lines: three publickey, three password, from svc_backup, jsmith and ops.admin. Rest the cursor on the second line, the 03:52:34 line, Accepted password for svc_backup, and say you will come back to it. Rest the cursor on the password lines and say an IP that failed and then got in needs its account checked, so those IPs are compared in the sheet first.
steps.type:
grep -c "Failed password" auth-jump01.log
grep -c "invalid user" auth-jump01.log
grep 'Accepted' auth-jump01.log
say: "Step 3: the failures, as a number to hit. I head straight down to the fresh prompt line at the bottom of the Terminal window, and I'm typing grep, dash c, then Failed password in double quotes, the log name, and Return, which counts every line with that phrase."
"Okay, 53, and my cursor rests right on it in the output. So 53 lines are failed passwords, and that's the total the pivot has to land on later."

"Now a second one just underneath. I drift on down beside that next prompt line, and I'm typing the same grep dash c, but with invalid user in quotes this time, and Return, because I want the tries on accounts that don't exist on this server."
"Fourteen, and I slide on down onto it in the output. So 14 of those tries were on usernames that aren't real accounts, which says somebody was guessing names, not just fumbling a password."

"So I've got two numbers to carry forward, my cursor going between the 53 and the 14. The 53 is the bar for the pivot, and if it comes out different, something's missing and I'd check my grep. The 14 just shows how much of this is name guessing."

"Next, who actually got in. I slide on down the left side of the text to the new prompt, and I'm typing grep once more, with Accepted inside single quotes, then the log name, and Return, so every successful login prints in one list."

"Right, six Accepted lines, three publickey and three password. My cursor runs down them, and the names are svc_backup, jsmith and ops.admin, with ops.admin on all three publickey lines. It's the password ones I'll focus on."
"Let me rest the pointer right on the second line down, 03:52:34, Accepted password for svc_backup. Hmm, that's a password login, so I'll come back to that one later."

"So here's how I'll handle those, with my cursor resting on the password lines. If an address failed first and then got in, that needs a look at the account, and Terminal can't show that cleanly. I'll compare them in the sheet, next to the failures, before I decide."

say: "Step 5: before I build anything, I want to see what's here. Row 1 first, and I'm sliding my cursor from A1 along to G1 as I read it: timestamp, host, event, user, invalid user, src ip and decision. So src ip is column F, the one I'll filter on."
"Then column G, the decision column. I run on down it, and it's empty the whole way, so nothing's been decided yet."
"To see where the data ends, I'm holding Command and pressing Down. That jumps to the last row, and my cursor rests on the number at the left edge, which says 60."
"Sixty rows, minus the header, is 59 rows of data, and my line count from earlier was 59 too. Same number, so nothing got dropped on the way in."

"Alright, that's the size confirmed, so I'm holding Command and pressing Up, and the view jumps back to the top row, with the pointer resting on the row 1 number at the left edge, ready for the next job."

steps.title: Build the pivot table
steps.window: Google Sheets: Insert menu, Create pivot table box, then the pivot editor on the right
steps.do: Move down to cell A1 and click it. Pause 1 s after "clicking it". Press Command A while speaking, with no pause, then move up to the name box at the top left and read it: A1:G60. Move up to Insert in the menu bar and open it. Pause 1 s after "opens its list". Move down the Insert list to Pivot table and choose it. Pause 1 s after "I select it". In the Create pivot table box pick New sheet. Pause 1 s after "choosing New sheet". Click Create at the bottom right of the box with a left click. Pause 1 s after "a left click". Slide the cursor along the bottom tabs onto Pivot Table 1, then up to the editor open on the right. Think aloud: one formula per pair is a lot of typing and a pivot counts them all at once, so the pivot. In the editor click Add beside Rows. Pause 1 s after "clicking there". In the list that drops down move to src_ip and click it. Pause 1 s after "choosing it". Move further down to Columns and click its Add button with a left click. Pause 1 s after "clicking that". From the list select event. Pause 1 s after "I pick event". Lower on the Columns card untick Show totals. Pause 1 s after "unticking it". Slide the cursor along the pivot's header row from left to right: Accepted password, Accepted publickey, Failed password. Move down to Values and click its Add button. Pause 1 s after "clicking that". In the list pick event. Pause 1 s after "pick event". Look lower on the value card at the Summarize by box to see what it is set to. If it already reads COUNTA, leave it and say so. Only if it reads SUM: open that dropdown, move down to COUNTA and pick it. Pause 1 s after "pick it". Say that each log line is one attempt, so COUNTA fits. Slide the cursor down the pivot to the Grand Total row at the bottom as the counts fill in.
say: "Step 7: the pivot table. First the selection needs to start in the corner, so I'm moving my cursor to A1, the top left cell of the grid, and clicking it."
"Command A selects the whole range, and then my cursor goes up to the name box at the top left, which now says A1 to G60, so every row and every column is in."
"Over to the menu bar again, to Insert this time, and a left click on it opens its list."
"I'm sliding down the Insert list, past the items above, to Pivot table. I want one row per address with a count for each event type, and that's what a pivot gives me, so I select it."
"A Create pivot table box opens in the middle, offering a new sheet or an existing one, and I'm choosing New sheet, so the data tab stays exactly as it is."
"Then I go over to the Create button, at the bottom right of the box, and a left click builds it, because I want the pivot on a tab of its own, where it can't disturb the raw rows."
"And a new tab has appeared along the bottom, called Pivot Table 1, so I slide across the tabs to it and then up to the editor open on the right."

"Let me think for a second, with my cursor drifting across the grid toward the tabs at the bottom. I could type a COUNTIF for every address and event pair, but that's a lot of typing, and a pivot counts them all in one go, so pivot it is."
"In the editor on the right there's a Rows section with an Add button, so I'm moving over to that and clicking there, because the addresses need to run down the side."
"A list drops down with the column names, and I'm moving down it to src underscore ip and choosing it. That groups the rows by source address."
"Further down the editor is Columns, with an Add button of its own. I'm moving down to it and clicking that, so the event types can go across the top."
"In this list I pick event, since that's the type of each attempt, and every type then gets a column of its own."
"Lower down on that Columns card there's a Show totals checkbox. I'm unticking it, because I don't need a row total, since the Failed password column already holds the failures."
"Along the pivot's header row, then, I slide on across from left to right, and it reads Accepted password, Accepted publickey, then Failed password, one column for each event type."
"Next, Values. A bit further down the editor there's a Values section with its own Add button, and I'm clicking that to tell the pivot what to count."
"I pick event again in this list, because every log row has one, so counting event is the same as counting rows."
"Lower on this value card is a Summarize by box, so I go on down to it, to see what it's set to."
"And it already reads COUNTA, which is exactly what I want, so I'll leave it alone."
"If it had said SUM, I'd open that dropdown, go down to COUNTA and pick it."
"COUNTA is right for this because every log line is one attempt, and it counts how many entries sit under each address and event, which is exactly the tally I'm after."
"And there are the counts, filling in on the left, and I run on down the pivot to a Grand Total row at the very bottom."

"Okay, now I'm running my cursor down the Failed password column, from the top address row to the bottom one, and the counts go 18, 14, 9, 7, 3 and 2."
"So that's the order I'll walk them in, with the pointer resting on the first address row, most failures to fewest, and the 18 gets judged first, because the biggest pile is the biggest risk."

Click OK at the bottom right of the panel with a left click. Pause 1 s after "a left click". Drag down column F over the filtered cells, first cell to last, so they all highlight. Slide the cursor from the selected cells to the count at the bottom right: 18, every row a Failed password. Run the cursor along columns D and E: root and admin in D, no in E on every row, 01:12:00 to 01:16:05, and no Accepted line. Hold the cursor on column D and say the verdict: Block.
say: "Step 9: the top address, 18 failures. The pivot only has counts and I want usernames and times, so I head over to the bottom left, and I'm clicking the auth-jump01-excerpt tab to get the raw rows back."
"Up in row 1, F1 is the src_ip header, with a small filter icon at its right edge, so I'm moving up to that icon and clicking that, and a list of values opens."
"At the top of that panel, under Filter by values, there's a Clear link, so I'm pressing Clear. That unticks every address, and I can pick exactly one."
"Now I go down the list of addresses, all the way to the sixth and last entry, and I tick that one. It's the address with the most failures, so only its rows should come back."
"Then to the OK button, at the bottom right of the panel, and a left click applies the filter."
"Now I'm dragging down column F, from the first filtered cell to the last, so they all highlight, and there's a count in the bottom right corner of the window."
"I drop down to that bottom right corner, and the count says 18, one for every row. So all 18 are this address."

"Across the rows now. Column D is root and admin, root 11 times and admin 7. Column E says no on every row, so these are real account names, and column A runs from 01:12:00 to 01:16:05, about four minutes, with nothing Accepted."

"So, the verdict on 203.0.113.45, and I'm holding on column D. It had 18 failures, root 11 times and admin 7, all inside about four minutes, from outside with no login, and those are the names guessing scripts try most. That fits my rule, so the call is Block."

steps.title: Last look, check and epilogue
steps.window: Google Sheets: Pivot Table 1 still on screen, Dock on the left
steps.do: The pivot is still on screen. Slide the cursor down the address column, then across to the Decision column: six addresses ranked, a decision beside each. Run the cursor down the Failed password column, then across each row to its Decision cell: Block beside 18 and 14, Watch beside 9 and 7, Ignore beside 3 and 2; the six add up to 53, the same as Terminal. Then say the closing paragraph as one single block, moving the cursor on the pivot as the spoken words reach each figure: the Decision column and the Grand Total, the 53; the bottom tabs; the Data menu; the header row; the first address row and its 18 and the 14; the Block pair; the Watch pair with their 9 and 7; the Ignore pair with their 3 and 2; the whole table from its top-left cell to the last Decision cell; the File menu; the two Watch rows; the header row again; then the Decision cells for Block 2, Watch 2 and Ignore 2. At the end slide left off the grid and rest on the Dock at the left edge until the paragraph ends.
say: "Step 18: the pivot's still up, so this is the last look. My cursor runs down the address column and across to the Decision column: six addresses ranked down the left, a decision beside each."

"Now the verdicts against the counts, down the Failed password column and across each row to its decision. Block sits beside 18 and 14, Watch beside 9 and 7, Ignore beside 3 and 2, and those add up to 53, matching the grep from earlier."

"So, start to finish, here's what I did. I began with the raw log and counted it: 59 lines, 53 of them Failed password, and 14 of those on usernames that don't exist. I did that first so I'd have numbers to check the sheet against. Then I went to the sheet, made sure all 59 rows had come in, froze the header, added a filter from the Data menu, and built a pivot with the source address down the side and the event types across the top. Its failure total came to 53, the same as my first count, so I trusted it, and only then did I start judging addresses. I went down the ranking from the biggest count, filtering the top two to read their usernames and times and reading the other four straight off the pivot, then typed a verdict beside each. The Block pair are the two biggest piles, 18 failures and 14, both from outside with no login. That fits my rule: an outside address with five or more failures and no login gets blocked for 24 hours. The Watch pair failed 9 times and 7 times and then got in, one as svc_backup and one as jsmith. I didn't block those, because a block could lock out a real person and a guessed password could still be live, so they get a password reset for svc_backup and a check with jsmith. The Ignore pair is the internal admin, who failed three times and then logged in, plus one outside address with just 2 tries, which is noise. Then I copied the table into the note, wrote an action line for each group, and checked the paste and the verdicts against the counts. After that I downloaded the note as a Word file and the sheet as an Excel file, and both landed in the browser's downloads. The hard part was telling Watch from Block when an address failed and then got in, because the counts alone couldn't separate a lucky guess from the real user. Next time I'd add the first and last attempt times to the pivot, to see how long after the last failure the login came. So for the goal: before the morning standup, last night's failed logins on jump01 are sorted. Block 2, Watch 2, Ignore 2, and the note tells the firewall owner what to act on, what to watch, and what to leave alone."
